options.a: Advise signers on which legal document best fits their situation
options.b: Deter fraud by verifying identity and witnessing signatures/oaths
options.c: Certify that the document's contents are true and legally valid
options.d: Act as an impartial witness who also explains the document's effects

distractorExplanations.a: Choosing documents for signers is legal advice, which is unauthorized practice of law for a non-attorney notary.
distractorExplanations.c: A notary verifies the signer's identity and signature, not the truth or legality of the document's contents.
distractorExplanations.d: Impartial witnessing is right, but explaining a document's legal effects is unauthorized practice of law.

notary-public-readiness-check-duties-001.explanation: Deter fraud by verifying identity and witnessing signatures/oaths as authorized. Notaries act only as authorized by their commissioning state.

options.a: Federal notary law issued by the U.S. Secretary of State
options.b: Their employer's written notarization policy above state law
options.c: State notary law and commissioning rules
options.d: The notary rules of whichever state the signer lives in

distractorExplanations.a: There is no general federal notary statute; notaries are commissioned and regulated by their state.
distractorExplanations.b: Employer policy cannot override state notary law; the notary's duties come from the commissioning state.
distractorExplanations.d: Notaries follow their own commissioning state's law, not the law of the signer's state of residence.

options.a: Signer swore under oath that the document's contents are true
options.b: Signer's document was found legally sufficient
options.c: Signer appeared, was identified, and acknowledged signing
options.d: Signer signed in front of the notary on the date of the act

distractorExplanations.a: Swearing to the truth of the contents describes a jurat, not an acknowledgment.
distractorExplanations.b: Notaries do not judge legal sufficiency; an acknowledgment certifies appearance, identity and acknowledged signing.
distractorExplanations.d: An acknowledgment does not require signing in the notary's presence; the signer acknowledges a signature already made.

options.a: Signer swearing/affirming truth and signing in notary presence
options.b: Signer acknowledging an earlier signature without taking an oath
options.c: Notary certifying a photocopy matches the original
options.d: Signer swearing to the truth and mailing the signed document later

distractorExplanations.b: That describes an acknowledgment; a jurat requires an oath or affirmation and signing in the notary's presence.
distractorExplanations.c: That is copy certification, a separate notarial act where authorized, not a jurat.
distractorExplanations.d: A jurat requires the signer to sign in the notary's presence, not to sign elsewhere and mail it in.

options.a: Notarize for a stranger
options.b: Notarize for a coworker or neighbor
options.c: Notarize their own signature
options.d: Charge a fee within the state limit

distractorExplanations.a: Notaries serve the public, including strangers, once identity is properly verified.
distractorExplanations.b: Notarizing for a coworker or neighbor is generally allowed when the notary has no interest in the transaction.
distractorExplanations.d: Charging fees up to the state maximum is generally permitted; overcharging is the violation.

options.a: Must meet state requirements
options.b: May be used by the employer
options.c: Follows one federal design
options.d: Belongs to the signer's file

distractorExplanations.b: The seal belongs to the notary and stays under the notary's exclusive control, even if the employer paid for it.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no federal seal standard; design, ink and content requirements are set by each state.
distractorExplanations.d: The seal is the notary's official tool, not part of the signer's record or file.

options.a: Signer/document determines; notary doesn’t give UPL advice
options.b: Notary selects the act that best protects the signer's interests
options.c: Employer selects the act to keep the office workflow consistent
options.d: Notary picks a jurat whenever the signer seems unsure

distractorExplanations.b: Choosing the act for a signer is legal advice (UPL); the signer or the document's drafter decides.
distractorExplanations.c: Employer preference does not determine the notarial act; the signer or the document's instructions do.
distractorExplanations.d: Defaulting to a jurat still has the notary choosing; an unsure signer should ask the drafter or an attorney.

options.a: Certifies the original's contents are true
options.b: Certifies copy of certain documents per state law
options.c: Authenticates the document for use in a foreign country
options.d: Certifies copies of birth and death certificates on request

distractorExplanations.a: Copy certification attests that the copy matches the original, not that the original's statements are true.
distractorExplanations.c: Foreign-use authentication is an apostille issued by a state official, not a notarial copy certification.
distractorExplanations.d: Vital records are usually excluded; certified copies come from the issuing vital records office.

options.a: Penalties only if a fee was charged
options.b: No liability if bonded by the state
options.c: Liability/commission problems
options.d: A warning letter with no further action

distractorExplanations.a: Negligence liability and commission discipline do not depend on whether the notary charged a fee.
distractorExplanations.b: A surety bond protects the public up to its amount; the notary can still be personally liable and disciplined.
distractorExplanations.d: Negligence can bring civil liability and commission suspension or revocation, not just a warning letter.

options.a: Must be translated into English by the notary first
options.b: May need caution; follow state rules
options.c: Are refused under federal notary law
options.d: Need a certified translator to sign as witness

distractorExplanations.a: Notaries are not required to translate, and translating legal text can itself be unauthorized practice of law.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no federal ban; state rules govern whether and how foreign-language documents are notarized.
distractorExplanations.d: A translator witness is not a general requirement; follow the commissioning state's specific rules.

notary-public-readiness-check-duties-012.explanation: May need caution; follow state rules; don’t explain legal meaning if UPL. Do not explain the document's legal meaning, which would be unauthorized practice of law.

options.a: Allowed anywhere once the signer consents
options.b: Only if state-authorized and technology compliant
options.c: Allowed for any notary using common video-call software
options.d: Allowed if the notary holds a federal e-notary permit

distractorExplanations.a: Signer consent is not enough; the notary's own state must authorize e-notarization and approved technology.
distractorExplanations.c: E-notarization requires state authorization and compliant technology, not just any video software.
distractorExplanations.d: There is no federal e-notary permit; authorization comes from the notary's commissioning state.

options.a: Set/limited by state rules
options.b: Set by the employer's price list
options.c: Set by a federal fee schedule
options.d: Set freely by each notary

distractorExplanations.b: Employers cannot set fees above the state maximum; fee limits come from state law.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no federal notary fee schedule; each state sets its own maximum fees.
distractorExplanations.d: Most states cap notary fees; notaries cannot charge any amount they choose.

options.a: Continue during a 30-day grace period
options.b: Continue using the old seal until it wears out
options.c: Stop notarizing until renewed
options.d: Continue if the renewal application is pending

distractorExplanations.a: There is generally no grace period; notarizing after expiration is an unauthorized act.
distractorExplanations.b: The seal is tied to the commission term; once the commission expires, it may not be used.
distractorExplanations.d: A pending application does not authorize acts; wait until the new commission takes effect.

options.a: A signed credit or debit card
options.b: A student ID with a photo and signature
options.c: A utility bill showing the signer's name
options.d: Government photo ID per state list

distractorExplanations.a: Credit cards lack the government-issued photo and physical description most states require.
distractorExplanations.b: Most state lists require government-issued ID; private student IDs usually do not qualify.
distractorExplanations.c: A utility bill shows a name and address, not photo identity; it is not satisfactory evidence of identity.

options.a: Acceptable if the photo still resembles the signer
options.b: Follow state rule—often unacceptable
options.c: OK if a second expired ID matches
options.d: Acceptable once the signer also signs the journal

distractorExplanations.a: Resemblance does not cure expiration; whether expired ID is accepted depends on the state's rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Two expired IDs do not equal one current ID; use state-approved alternatives such as credible witnesses.
distractorExplanations.d: A journal signature does not prove identity; acceptability of expired ID is set by state rule.

options.a: Date, signer's name, and fee, with ID details left optional
options.b: Signer's name, document contents summary, and legal advice given
options.c: Date, document type, and signer's Social Security number
options.d: Date, type of act, document, ID, fees, signature/thumb as required

distractorExplanations.a: The method and details of identification are core journal entries wherever journals are required.
distractorExplanations.b: Journals record the act and ID, not a summary of contents or legal advice, which notaries may not give.
distractorExplanations.c: SSNs are not standard journal entries and create privacy risk; the ID type and number are recorded instead.

options.a: Property of the employer who paid
options.b: A public file anyone can browse
options.c: A personal diary of daily tasks
options.d: Notary’s official record—protect it

distractorExplanations.a: In most states the journal belongs to the notary even if the employer paid for it.
distractorExplanations.b: Some states allow inspection of specific entries on request, but the journal is protected, not open for browsing.
distractorExplanations.c: The journal is an official record of notarial acts, not a personal diary of the notary's work.

options.a: Notify authorities/state as required
options.b: Recreate the missing entries from memory
options.c: Report it at commission renewal
options.d: Tell only the employer's manager

distractorExplanations.b: Recreating entries falsifies the record; report the loss as state law requires.
distractorExplanations.c: Loss or theft must be reported promptly (often within days), not saved until renewal.
distractorExplanations.d: The employer is not the regulator; notify the commissioning authority and police as required.

options.a: Appear in person
options.b: Appear by phone call
options.c: Send a signed copy
options.d: Send a trusted relative

distractorExplanations.b: A phone call is not personal appearance; authorized RON uses audio-video and identity proofing.
distractorExplanations.c: Mailing a signed copy skips personal appearance and identity verification.
distractorExplanations.d: A relative cannot appear in the signer's place; the signer must personally appear.

notary-public-readiness-check-id-journal.explanation: Appear in person (unless remote online notary rules apply) Remote online notarization is the exception where state rules allow it.

options.a: ID the first signer; vouch for others
options.b: ID each; use one journal line for all
options.c: ID each; skip the journal for spouses
options.d: ID each; complete proper certificates

distractorExplanations.a: Each signer must be identified; one person's ID does not cover the other signers.
distractorExplanations.b: Journal rules generally require a separate entry and signature for each signer.
distractorExplanations.c: Spouses are separate signers and each needs a journal entry where journals are required.

options.a: Be a party named in the document
options.b: Be a relative who lives with the signer
options.c: Be identified and meet state criteria
options.d: Be the notary's coworker on duty

distractorExplanations.a: Credible witnesses must generally have no interest in the transaction; a named party is disqualified.
distractorExplanations.b: Relationship is not the test; the witness must meet state criteria, usually including personally knowing the signer.
distractorExplanations.d: Convenience is not a qualification; a credible witness must know the signer and meet state rules.

options.a: Required federally for every act
options.b: Required for every jurat signer
options.c: State-specific (e.g., some deeds)
options.d: Required for signers without ID

distractorExplanations.a: There is no federal thumbprint rule; a few states (e.g., California for certain deeds) require it.
distractorExplanations.b: Thumbprints are tied to specific documents in certain states, not to jurats in general.
distractorExplanations.d: Missing ID is handled through credible witnesses, not thumbprints; requirements are state-specific.

options.a: Signer has not read the full document before signing it
options.b: Signer brings a document that was drafted by an out-of-state lawyer
options.c: Signer cannot be identified / appears coerced / act unauthorized
options.d: Signer is a non-customer of the notary's employer bank

distractorExplanations.a: Notaries do not require signers to read documents; refusal grounds are identity, willingness, or authority problems.
distractorExplanations.b: Out-of-state drafting is no reason to refuse; documents for use in other states are routinely notarized.
distractorExplanations.d: Non-customer status is not a legal ground for refusal; refusal centers on identity, willingness, and authority.

options.a: Comply if signed
options.b: Stamp, date later
options.c: Refuse—illegal
options.d: Comply for staff

distractorExplanations.a: A later signature does not fix a blank notarization; the signer must appear and be identified at the time.
distractorExplanations.b: Dating a certificate later is backdating or blank certification, both forms of misconduct.
distractorExplanations.d: Employees get no exception; notarizing blank certificates is illegal for anyone.

options.a: Hold the ID up to any video camera for viewing
options.b: Use knowledge questions only, without credential checks
options.c: Follow approved methods if commissioned for RON
options.d: Follow RON methods even without a RON commission

distractorExplanations.a: Viewing an ID on camera alone is not enough; RON requires approved credential analysis and identity proofing.
distractorExplanations.b: Knowledge-based questions are usually paired with credential analysis; one method alone generally fails RON rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Notaries must be authorized or registered for RON in their state before performing remote acts.

options.a: Notarize if the last names match, ignoring first-name spelling
options.b: Notarize under the ID name and cross out the document name
options.c: Resolve carefully per law; may require corrected docs
options.d: Have the signer sign both names to cover the mismatch

distractorExplanations.a: Name variances must satisfy state rules; matching only part of a name is not enough.
distractorExplanations.b: Notaries may not alter the document; corrected documents or state-permitted variance rules apply.
distractorExplanations.d: Signing two names does not resolve identity; follow state name-variance rules or obtain corrected documents.

options.a: Complete journal contemporaneously
options.b: Complete the journal at day's end
options.c: Let the signer fill in the journal
options.d: Complete it only for paid acts

distractorExplanations.b: End-of-day entries rely on memory; entries are made at the time of each notarization.
distractorExplanations.c: The notary is responsible for entries; the signer typically just signs where required.
distractorExplanations.d: Journal entries are needed for every notarial act where journals are required, not just paid ones.

options.a: Match the signer's request
options.b: Use the employer's template
options.c: Follow federal standard text
options.d: Match the act performed

distractorExplanations.a: The signer may choose the act, but the wording must match the act actually performed.
distractorExplanations.b: Templates must still carry state-required wording for the act actually performed.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no federal certificate form; wording follows state law for the specific act.

options.a: Stamp the page and sign without certificate wording
options.b: Choose and attach the act you think the signer needs
options.c: Write a short note that the document was notarized
options.d: Attach/complete a proper loose certificate if allowed

distractorExplanations.a: A seal and signature without certificate wording is not a complete notarial certificate.
distractorExplanations.b: Choosing the act for the signer is legal advice; the signer must say which certificate is needed.
distractorExplanations.c: Informal notes are not valid certificates; state-compliant certificate wording is required.

options.a: Use correction fluid neatly and re-stamp the seal
options.b: Change the date to match when the signer wanted it
options.c: Follow lawful correction practices; never falsify
options.d: Let the signer fix errors after the seal is applied

distractorExplanations.a: Correction fluid on certificates is generally prohibited; corrections follow state-approved practices.
distractorExplanations.b: Changing the date to anything other than the actual act date is backdating, which is falsification.
distractorExplanations.d: The notary corrects the certificate under state rules; signers may not alter it after sealing.

options.a: The date the act occurred
options.b: The date the document was signed
options.c: The date on the document heading
options.d: The date the journal was reviewed

distractorExplanations.b: For acknowledgments the signature may predate the act; the certificate date is the notarization date.
distractorExplanations.c: The document's own date may differ; the certificate records when the notarial act occurred.
distractorExplanations.d: Journal review dates are irrelevant; the certificate states the actual date of the notarial act.

options.a: Clear and legible
options.b: Placed over signatures
options.c: Embossed only, no ink
options.d: On a separate blank page

distractorExplanations.b: Seals should not cover signatures or text, which can make the document unreadable.
distractorExplanations.c: Many states require an inked seal that photocopies clearly; embossing alone often does not comply.
distractorExplanations.d: Not the best answer: On a separate blank page only always.

options.a: Depends on the notary's preference
options.b: Jurat whenever the document is a deed
options.c: Depends on document/instructions
options.d: Acknowledgment for every signer

distractorExplanations.a: The notary may not choose the act; doing so would be unauthorized legal advice.
distractorExplanations.b: Deeds usually call for acknowledgments, not jurats; the document or signer determines the act.
distractorExplanations.d: There is no default act; the document's wording or the signer's instructions determine it.

notary-public-readiness-check-certificat.explanation: Depends on document/instructions—notary doesn’t choose to change meaning casually. The notary does not choose the act or change the document's meaning.

options.a: Different roles—don’t confuse
options.b: Same role, same legal effect
options.c: Notary also signs as a witness
options.d: Two witnesses replace a notary

distractorExplanations.b: A subscribing witness and a notary perform distinct roles with different legal effects.
distractorExplanations.c: A notary does not automatically act as a subscribing witness; that is a separate role with its own rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Witness requirements and notarization are separate; witnesses do not substitute for a required notarization.

options.a: A notarial act for use in another U.S. state
options.b: Authentication for international use
options.c: A certificate the notary attaches for foreign use
options.d: A translation certificate for foreign documents

distractorExplanations.a: Interstate documents generally need no apostille; apostilles authenticate documents for Hague Convention countries.
distractorExplanations.c: The notary does not issue apostilles; the Secretary of State (or U.S. Department of State) does.
distractorExplanations.d: An apostille authenticates a public official's signature or seal; it is not a translation certificate.

notary-public-readiness-check-certificat.explanation: Authentication for international use—usually not the notary’s act itself. It is usually issued by a state official, not the notary's own act.

options.a: May complete a jurat if the signer re-swears
options.b: Can complete an acknowledgment without appearance
options.c: Need a witness in place of the jurat oath
options.d: Generally cannot complete jurat

distractorExplanations.a: A jurat requires signing in the notary's presence; re-swearing does not cure an out-of-presence signature.
distractorExplanations.b: Acknowledgments allow prior signing but still require the signer to appear before the notary.
distractorExplanations.c: Witnesses do not replace the oath or the in-presence signing that a jurat requires.

notary-public-readiness-check-certificat.explanation: Generally cannot complete jurat; follow acknowledgment rules carefully. Follow acknowledgment rules carefully for documents already signed.

options.a: Must meet state e-notary standards
options.b: Can be any scanned seal image
options.c: Can be shared with the employer
options.d: Follow one federal e-seal format

distractorExplanations.b: Scanned images without security controls fail state e-notary standards for tamper-evidence.
distractorExplanations.c: Electronic seals and signatures must stay under the notary's sole control.
distractorExplanations.d: There is no federal e-seal format; electronic seal standards come from the commissioning state.

options.a: Stapled to a separate copy of the document
options.b: Securely associated with the document
options.c: Kept in the notary's journal for safety
options.d: Left for the recipient to attach

distractorExplanations.a: The loose certificate is attached to the original signed document, not to a separate copy.
distractorExplanations.c: The certificate must accompany the document; the journal records the act, not loose certificates.
distractorExplanations.d: Blank or unattached certificates invite fraud; the notary completes and attaches them.

options.a: Complete it if they sign
options.b: Do not complete jurat
options.c: Seal it and note refusal
options.d: Switch to acknowledgment

distractorExplanations.a: A signature without an oath or affirmation does not satisfy a jurat.
distractorExplanations.c: Noting the refusal does not make the jurat valid; it cannot be completed without the oath.
distractorExplanations.d: The notary may not swap the act on their own; the signer or document determines which act applies.

options.a: Means the notary certifies the agent's authority
options.b: May require extra care/ID of capacity docs per rules
options.c: Requires the notary to draft the POA document
options.d: Allows the agent to sign without showing ID

distractorExplanations.a: Most notaries do not certify representative capacity; they identify the signer and follow state rules.
distractorExplanations.c: Drafting a power of attorney is legal work; the notary only notarizes the agent's signature.
distractorExplanations.d: The agent must still be identified like any signer; representative capacity does not waive ID.

options.a: A civil issue only
options.b: A serious offense
options.c: A minor rule breach
options.d: Legal if signer OKs

distractorExplanations.a: Fraudulent certificates can bring criminal charges, not just civil liability.
distractorExplanations.c: False certificates are typically crimes and grounds for revocation, not minor rule breaches.
distractorExplanations.d: Signer consent does not legalize a fraudulent certificate; it is still a false official statement.

options.a: The signer is a long-time customer of the notary's employer
options.b: They are a party to the transaction or have disqualifying interest
options.c: They notarized a different document for the signer last week
options.d: The document will be recorded in a different county

distractorExplanations.a: A customer relationship is not a disqualifying interest; a financial or beneficial interest is.
distractorExplanations.c: Prior notarizations for the same person create no conflict of interest.
distractorExplanations.d: Where a document is recorded does not affect the notary's authority to notarize it within the state.

notary-public-readiness-check-misconduct.explanation: They are a party to the transaction or have disqualifying interest (state rules) Disqualification rules vary by state.

options.a: Allowed if minor
options.b: Misconduct
options.c: OK if requested
options.d: A clerical issue

distractorExplanations.a: Backdating is falsification of an official certificate no matter how few days are involved.
distractorExplanations.c: A signer's request does not authorize a false date on a notarial certificate.
distractorExplanations.d: Backdating is a false statement on an official certificate, not a clerical issue.

options.a: Allowed for notarios publicos
options.b: Allowed if the notary only fills forms
options.c: Unauthorized practice / unlawful
options.d: Allowed with a bilingual notary seal

distractorExplanations.a: U.S. notaries are not Latin American 'notarios'; that title confusion is exactly what UPL laws target.
distractorExplanations.b: Filling out immigration forms for others is regulated immigration consulting, not a notary power.
distractorExplanations.d: Language ability or a seal does not authorize immigration advice; it remains unauthorized practice.

options.a: Allowed if the signer phones in to confirm identity
options.b: Allowed if the signature looks genuine
options.c: Generally prohibited (except authorized RON)
options.d: Allowed if a relative brings the ID

distractorExplanations.a: Phone confirmation is not personal appearance; authorized RON is the exception to physical presence.
distractorExplanations.b: Signature appearance cannot replace personal appearance and identity verification.
distractorExplanations.d: A relative presenting ID does not make the signer present; the signer must appear.

options.a: Allowed once the commission ends
options.b: May violate retention rules
options.c: Allowed after one calendar year
options.d: Protects signer privacy best

distractorExplanations.a: Many states require retention or surrender of journals after the commission ends, not destruction.
distractorExplanations.c: Retention periods are set by state law and often run many years, not one year.
distractorExplanations.d: Privacy is protected by securing the journal, not by destroying it before required retention ends.

options.a: Keep notarizing with a backup stamp
options.b: Notify state as required; obtain replacement
options.c: Report it only at commission renewal
options.d: Order a new seal without notifying the state

distractorExplanations.a: A lost seal must be reported first; using a duplicate without notice invites fraud.
distractorExplanations.c: Lost seals must be reported promptly as state rules require, not saved until renewal.
distractorExplanations.d: Replacement alone leaves the lost seal open to misuse; the state (and often police) must be notified.

options.a: Detailed personal memory of each signer and document
options.b: A large surety bond and liability waiver
options.c: Proper ID, complete journal, correct certificates
options.d: Signer-signed statements after each act

distractorExplanations.a: Memory fades; contemporaneous journal records and correct certificates are the real defense.
distractorExplanations.b: A bond protects the public and a waiver does not excuse misconduct; documented procedure is the defense.
distractorExplanations.d: Signer statements do not replace proper ID checks, journal entries and correct certificates.
